newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S., China keys to Asian peace, says Hashimoto.
newsitem.headline: U.S., China keys to Asian peace, says Hashimoto.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Tuesday peace and progress in Asia depended on a continued U.S. military presence and making China into a constructive member of the international community.

"I am convinced that the presence of a politically stable, economically prosperous China, bound by ties of trust with the rest of the world, would be in everybody's interest," he said in a major foreign policy address.
"Now that China has been following a path of modernization through its policy of reform and openness, she takes more part in every area," he said.

"It is important for the rest of the world to support the policy direction and to enhance wide-ranging dialogues and exchanges with China, so she can secure her position as a constructive partner in the international community."
Hashimoto said at the end of a five-nation visit to Southeast Asia that to secure peace in the region, the most important factor was the U.S. presence.

"Several unstable factors persist in the region, so that these factors will not become international conflicts, the presence of the United States, a country of unrivalled power and founded upon principles such as democracy, market mechanisms and respect for creativity, is essential," he said.

Hashimoto did not identify the possible sources of conflict, but in answering questions after his speech, he called on China and Taiwan to make "a cool-headed attempt to try to resolve their problems through dialogue".

"We certainly would not welcome tensions in the Taiwan Strait," he added in an apparent reference to Chinese war games near the island last year that led to the United States sending two aircraft carrier battle groups to the area.

Taking relations between Japan and the seven-member Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) -- which groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- was also important, Hashimoto said.

"Given the increasing importance of ASEAN as an entity with one voice in the international community, I think it particularly necessary to strengthen policy dialogues between Japan and ASEAN at various levels," he said.
"Dialogues at top levels should be enhanced to build stronger personal ties of trust between top leaders," he added.
"I would like to take every possible opportunity to have closer and more frequent dialogues with my ASEAN partners."

Hashimoto said he went ahead with his visits to Brunei, Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam and Singapore despite the hostage crisis at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima because he believed Japan's ties with ASEAN needed a push.
Marxist rebels have been holding more than 70 hostages in Peru for four weeks.
Hashimoto said he had won agreement from the leaders he had met during his tour for regular Japan-ASEAN summits, which he told a news conference on Monday should be held at least once a year.
He also called for closer cooperation at the United Nations, where Japan is about to take a seat on the Security Council for two years.

"To ensure peace and stability in the Asia Pacific in the 21st Century, I would like to see Japan have frank dialogues on regional security with each of the ASEAN countries on a bilateral basis," Hashimoto added.
He did not elaborate on what that meant and when asked specifically about the idea after the speech, spoke only of seminars attended by senior military officers.
